sentences.text: The archive in the town was open on Tuesdays and Thursdays between ten and one, which she found out by walking there four times.
The woman behind the desk was called Dona Amparo and was not, at first, encouraging.
She said the tithe maps were not for handling.
She said there was an index.
She said what exactly was it that Sabela wanted.
Sabela said she wanted to know if there had been a road across her garden before 1890.
Dona Amparo looked at her for a second and then got up and went into the back room without another word, and came out seven minutes later with a flat grey box.
The map was enormous and the colours in it were still bright.
It was dated 1871.
It took them a while to find the house, because the house was smaller on the map than Sabela expected and because the field boundaries were all wrong, which was the point.
Dona Amparo found it in the end by working out from the church.
And there it was.

A double line, ruled, going down off the hill from the top left, through the plot that was now their garden, over the corner of what was now the Oteros' hayfield, along the edge of nothing in particular, down the bank at the place with the steps, and along the river to a small black rectangle labelled, in beautiful sloping brown ink, *Muíño*.
Sabela put her finger about a centimetre above the paper and traced it, and it was the line.
Every turn.
The distance-and-a-half past where the shed would be built in 1963.
The high part of the wall, which on the map was not a wall at all but the road's own edge.
"You knew where to look," said Dona Amparo.
"I followed a pig," said Sabela.
There was a pause of the particular kind that happens when an adult decides how to take something.
"Mm," said Dona Amparo, and turned the map round so it faced Sabela properly, and left her with it for the best part of an hour.
The boar still comes through the hedge.

He is older now — the notch in his ear has a second notch above it and he takes the bank at the river in two goes instead of one — but he comes at about ten past nine, most nights, and he walks the diagonal.
Sabela has photocopies of the 1871 sheet on her wall and a stone at each of the four points, which her mother has twice tidied away and twice put back after being told.
She has not told anyone at school.
She has thought about it and decided that it does not come out well when you say it, and that this is fine, and that the road is not less there for nobody looking at it.
That is, after all, exactly the situation it has been in since 1890.
